newsitem.title: USA: General Dynamics buying two Lockheed units for $450 million.
newsitem.headline: General Dynamics buying two Lockheed units for $450 million.

text.p: Defense company General Dynamics Corp., seeking to broaden its product line, said Thursday it will pay about $450 million in cash to acquire two units of Lockheed Martin Corp. that make combat vehicles and gun systems.

The Falls Church, Va.-based company specializes in making nuclear submarines, destroyer ships and heavy duty armored vehicles such as tanks. The acquisition will add medium and light armored vehicles to its product line when it closes by the end of the year.
General Dynamics said the units were expected to produce some $500 million in revenues this year and "significantly higher" revenues in 1997, immediately adding to its profits.

The two units include Lockheed Martin's armament systems unit, which has plants in Burlington, Vt. and Milan, Tenn., employing 1,600 people, and its defense systems unit in Pittsfield, Mass. which employs about 1,650.

The armament systems unit makes a variety of advanced gun systems. The defense systems business builds turrets and transmissions for combat vehicles, as well as missile guidance and naval fire control systems.
"This fits our strategy for our land systems business to broaden our product line in the armored vehicle business," said Paul Hesse, a General Dynamic spokesman.

Land systems accounts for about a third of General Dynamics' revenues, which totaled $3.06 billion in fiscal year 1995. Hesse said a decision had not yet been made on whether there will be any layoffs.
The deal is the General Dynamics' third major acquisition this year, after it bought shipbuilder Bath Iron Works and Teledyne Vehicle Systems.
Hesse said General Dynamics has about $1.1 billion cash in hand, allowing it to pay for the latest acquisition and consider making more.
"Our strategy is to consider further acquisitions as long as they are in areas which are related to our core businesses and core competencies," he said.
Hesse said the company's virtually debt-free balance sheet gives it the financial flexibility to consider larger deals, if it "makes sense from a shareholder point of view."

After years of mega-mergers, consolidation in the rapidly changing aerospace and defense industry is expected to continue, but on a smaller scale. Smaller deals, like this one, are expected to become more prevalent, experts said.
"There aren't that many big ones left," said Kent Newcomb, an analyst at brokerage A.G. Edwards.
He said McDonald Douglas Corp., Northrop Grumman Corp. and Lockheed are among those that are looking to make acquisitions in coming months.

Lockheed Martin Chief Executive Norman R. Augustine said the units being sold were not part of the firm's core business. Lockheed Martin, based in Bethesda, Md., specializes in electronics for military and civil applications.
Analysts said Lockheed's decision was also spurred by a desire to reduce its heavy $12 billion debt load, much of which stems from the $9.1 billion acquisition of Loral Corp. earlier this year.
General Dynamics's stock gained $1.25 to $68.50 in late trading on the New York Stock Exchange, while Lockheed Martin lost 62.5 cents to $89.75, also on the NYSE.
